Diagram-expansion terms describing gradient-flow regimes across width and parameterization.
Approach
Expands training dynamics into regime-specific terms that distinguish kernel-like and feature-learning behavior.
Themes
Mean-field theory; NTK regimes; representation movement.

SVRG and Beyond via Posterior Correction

ICML 2026

SVRG and Beyond via Posterior Correction reinterprets variance reduction as belief correction. A stochastic gradient is a noisy glimpse of the loss surface, and classical SVRG corrects that glimpse with a reference estimate. This paper asks what happens if the correction is treated as a posterior object that can carry richer uncertainty, including Hessian-like information. The concrete object is a Gaussian posterior over gradient and curvature correction terms. The first-principles problem is to use more local geometry without paying for full deterministic second-order optimization, so stochastic updates become better informed without losing scalability.

Mathematical object
A Gaussian posterior over stochastic gradient and Hessian correction terms.
Approach
Uses richer posterior correction families to generalize variance reduction beyond classical SVRG updates.
Themes
Stochastic optimization; posterior correction; second-order information.

FIRE

ICLR 2026

FIRE treats reinitialization as a measured reset of representation geometry. When adapting to a new task, a random reset can destroy useful structure, but no reset can leave the model trapped in a stale representation. The concrete object is representation geometry measured by deviation from isometry before and after reset. Newton-Schulz-based control calibrates how much geometry is reset across vision, language, and reinforcement-learning settings. The first-principles problem is plasticity without amnesia: restore enough freedom for new learning while preserving the structure that still helps.

Mathematical object
A representation geometry measured by deviation from isometry before and after reset.
Approach
Uses Newton-Schulz-based geometry control to calibrate reinitialization for stability and plasticity.
Themes
Reinitialization; stability-plasticity tradeoff; representation geometry.

LR Decay Wastes Your Best Data

ICML 2026

LR Decay Wastes Your Best Data argues that a strong example can arrive too late to matter. Data quality is not an absolute property, because the optimizer decides how much the model can still move when the example appears. After learning-rate decay, even useful evidence may produce only a tiny update. The concrete object is a training trajectory where example value is coupled to arrival time and step size. The paper studies how curriculum benefits can vanish under decay. The first-principles lesson is that data is time-dependent evidence: its effect depends on the movement budget still available.

Mathematical object
A training trajectory where example value is modulated by learning-rate schedule and arrival time.
Approach
Analyzes curriculum and LR-decay interactions to show when late high-quality data cannot move the model.
Themes
Curriculum learning; data value; optimizer schedules.

LoRA Gradient Descent

ICML 2026

LoRA Gradient Descent treats adapter fine-tuning as mathematics, not just a cheap trick. LoRA changes a model through low-rank factors, and those factors make the optimization landscape different from ordinary full-rank weight updates. The concrete object is the original LoRA parameterization optimized by gradient descent, with its stacked factors and non-smooth structure left intact. The paper proves convergence for the update people actually use. The first-principles value is that the practical parameterization receives its own theory, instead of being explained by a cleaner problem that no longer matches deployed fine-tuning.

Mathematical object
A low-rank adapter factorization optimized by gradient descent in its original parameterization.
Approach
Proves convergence despite the non-smooth structure of stacked low-rank adapter factors.
Themes
Low-rank adaptation; optimization theory; fine-tuning practice.

Polar Express

ICML 2026

Polar Express treats an optimizer step as matrix geometry, not only as a vector direction. In many neural layers, the update has singular structure and orthogonality properties that affect training, especially under low precision. The concrete object is a matrix-valued optimizer update shaped by polar decomposition and orthogonalization. Practical polar-decomposition machinery makes Muon-style updates stable enough for low-precision language-model training. The first-principles problem is update shape: training depends not only on where the step points, but on the matrix structure carried by the step.

Mathematical object
A matrix-valued optimizer update shaped by polar decomposition and orthogonalization.
Approach
Uses practical polar-decomposition machinery to produce stable orthogonalized updates in low precision.
Themes
Matrix optimizers; Muon-style updates; low-precision training.

Beyond Muon

ICML 2026

Beyond Muon treats a successful optimizer as one point in a larger design space, not as a universal rule. Orthogonalized matrix updates can help, but a compressed orthogonal direction is not always better than Adam-like adaptivity or scaling. The concrete object is a family of matrix optimizer updates spanning orthogonalized and adaptive behavior. The analysis compares when each update geometry helps or harms training. The first-principles problem is identifying the useful part of an optimizer: separate the benefit of matrix geometry from the cases where it becomes an overconstraint.

Mathematical object
A family of matrix optimizer updates spanning orthogonalized and Adam-like behavior.
Approach
Compares update geometries to identify when compressed orthogonal movement helps or harms training.
Themes
Optimizer families; update geometry; limits of recipe transfer.

LoRA-Pre

ICML 2026

LoRA-Pre treats optimizer memory as a compressible state with mathematical structure. Momentum stores past gradient information, but adapter training at scale can still make optimizer state expensive. The concrete object is a low-rank subspace representation of EMA momentum and historical gradients. Reframing momentum as online linear regression identifies what history must be retained for stable movement and what can be projected away. The first-principles problem is memory with purpose: keep the part of past gradients that guides the next update, not every stored number simply because the optimizer produced it.

Mathematical object
A low-rank subspace representation of optimizer momentum and historical gradient state.
Approach
Models EMA momentum as online regression and compresses optimizer state while preserving useful update history.
Themes
Optimizer memory; low-rank training; efficient adaptation.
BATCH 10

Optimization Under Constraints and Resources

SGD RLVR

ICML 2026

SGD RLVR asks whether reasoning post-training really needs a heavy adaptive optimizer. In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, the feedback is sparse but concrete: a solution can often be checked by execution, proof, or an external verifier. That changes the optimizer tradeoff. The concrete object is a policy-update trajectory under a memory budget, where rollout scale may matter more than Adam-style state. The paper shows that memory-efficient SGD can match or beat AdamW in this setting. The first-principles lesson is that optimizer choice depends on reward structure and memory pressure, not habit.

Mathematical object
A verifiable-reward policy optimization trajectory under memory-constrained SGD updates.
Approach
Compares lightweight SGD-style post-training against AdamW when the reward signal is executable or verifiable.
Themes
RL post-training; memory-efficient optimization; verifiable rewards.

RACO

ICML 2026

RACO treats learning with many objectives as movement through disagreement. Alignment, preference learning, safety, and distillation can combine losses whose gradients do not point toward the same improvement. The concrete object is a multi-objective gradient field with conflicts among objective-specific descent directions. Clipping and adjustment make the update conflict-averse while preserving convergence guarantees. The method asks which parts of each gradient can be trusted when objectives pull apart. The first-principles problem is controlled compromise: move without letting one objective erase another, but also avoid becoming frozen whenever objectives disagree.

Mathematical object
A multi-objective gradient field with conflicts among objective-specific descent directions.
Approach
Clips and adjusts updates so movement remains conflict-averse while retaining convergence guarantees.
Themes
Multi-objective optimization; alignment gradients; conflict-averse learning.

Global Merging

ICML 2026

Global Merging treats disagreement among distributed workers as something to interpret, not automatically erase. In decentralized training, different workers may hold harmful variance, but they may also explore complementary parts of the loss geometry. The concrete object is a set of decentralized model states with disagreement decomposed into noise and useful search signal. The analysis connects merging rules to parallel-SGD convergence rates. The first-principles problem is useful difference: a merge should remove destructive inconsistency while preserving the worker variation that improves the shared model.

Mathematical object
A set of decentralized model states with disagreement decomposed into noise and useful search signal.
Approach
Analyzes merging rules that match parallel-SGD rates by retaining the productive part of worker divergence.
Themes
Distributed optimization; model merging; decentralized training dynamics.

Non-Euclidean EoS

ICML 2026

Non-Euclidean EoS says that training stability cannot be understood only in the ordinary Euclidean picture of gradient descent. Modern optimizers normalize, precondition, block, spectralize, or limit updates by different norms, so the model is moving through parameter space with a different geometry. The concrete object is the edge-of-stability condition measured in the metric induced by the optimizer. The paper reframes sharpness as a relationship between loss curvature and the actual update rule, making instability a property of how the optimizer is allowed to move, not just a property of the loss surface.

Mathematical object
An edge-of-stability condition measured under optimizer-specific non-Euclidean metrics.
Approach
Generalizes stability diagnostics across normalized, preconditioned, block, spectral, and infinity-norm updates.
Themes
Training stability; optimizer geometry; sharpness diagnostics.

WSM

ICML 2026

WSM asks whether part of learning-rate decay is really checkpoint geometry. Decay is usually described as changing the step size over time, but the final model also reflects where training stops along a path of weights. The concrete object is a weighted average over checkpoints on that optimization trajectory. WSM constructs averaging rules that emulate cosine, linear, and inverse-square-root schedules without using the original schedule. The first-principles separation is between two effects: how large each update is when it happens, and which stable point along the traveled path is finally selected.

Mathematical object
A weighted model-average point over checkpoints along an optimization trajectory.
Approach
Constructs averaging rules that reproduce common learning-rate decay behavior without relying on the original schedule.
Themes
Model averaging; learning-rate schedules; trajectory geometry.

Dirac-Frenkel-Onsager

ICML 2026

Dirac-Frenkel-Onsager treats learning dynamics as movement of functions, not merely movement of coordinates. Many parameter velocities can describe the same change in model behavior, so parameter motion contains arbitrary degrees of freedom. The concrete object is a parameterized function-space path with multiple equivalent parameter velocities. The method uses Dirac-Frenkel-Onsager structure to choose smoother dynamics among those equivalent motions. The first-principles problem is separating behavior from coordinates: optimization theory should track how the represented function changes, not confuse that with accidental motion in one parameterization.

Mathematical object
A parameterized function-space path with multiple equivalent parameter velocities.
Approach
Uses Dirac-Frenkel-Onsager structure to select smoother dynamics among gauge-equivalent parameter motions.
Themes
Function-space optimization; gauge freedom; temporal learning dynamics.

Phase Retrieval Dynamics

ICML 2026

Phase Retrieval Dynamics treats training as a sequence of regimes controlled by the data spectrum. Nonlinear regression with anisotropic data does not improve at one uniform rate: early alignment can be fast, while late error depends on low-variance directions. The concrete object is a nonlinear regression trajectory decomposed by anisotropic spectral components. The analysis derives phase-wise dynamics under spectral decay. The first-principles problem is learning order: the optimizer first captures dominant structure, then pays the cost of weaker directions that still matter for final error.

Mathematical object
A nonlinear regression trajectory decomposed by anisotropic spectral components.
Approach
Derives phase-wise dynamics showing how spectral decay controls early alignment and late-stage error.
Themes
Learning phases; spectral decay; nonlinear regression dynamics.

Neural Thickets

ICML 2026

Neural Thickets changes the picture of fine-tuning. A base model is often treated as one general point that must be moved toward a task-specific solution. This paper instead views pretrained weights as sitting in a dense local neighborhood of nearby specialists. The concrete object is that neighborhood: small parameter moves that produce distinct task abilities. The first-principles question is why small updates can have large behavioral effects. The answer is that pretraining has already arranged a rich local region, so adaptation can be local search among nearby usable directions rather than a long trip through parameter space.

Mathematical object
A local neighborhood around pretrained weights containing many reachable task-specialist parameter vectors.
Approach
Analyzes the geometry of nearby specializations in large pretrained models to explain efficient adaptation.
Themes
Fine-tuning geometry; pretrained basins; local specialization.

DMS

ICML 2026

DMS improves how search systems compare high-dimensional distributions. Quality-diversity methods often rely on histogram-style discounting, but bins can hide meaningful differences between nearby measures or create artificial differences where the underlying distributions are close. The concrete object is a smooth distance-like comparison used to guide search allocation. Replacing brittle histograms with a differentiable measure-sensitive model gives the optimizer a signal tied to real distributional change. The first-principles question is where search effort should go: toward regions that add new behavior, not regions that only look new because the binning scheme changed.

Mathematical object
A smooth distance-like comparison between high-dimensional measures used by search or quality-diversity systems.
Approach
Replaces brittle histogram discounting with a differentiable measure-sensitive scoring model.
Themes
Distribution comparison; quality-diversity optimization; search allocation.

FlexRank

ICML 2026

FlexRank treats rank as a controllable resource for capability and cost. A model does not always need full-rank computation, but one fixed compressed rank can be too rigid when tasks vary across language, vision, and difficulty. The concrete object is a nested low-rank representation whose active rank changes with budget and capability needs. Selective activation lets the model spend more rank only where it helps. The first-principles problem is adjustable capacity: computation should expand for hard cases and shrink for easy ones without replacing the whole model.

Mathematical object
A nested low-rank representation whose active rank can vary with cost and capability needs.
Approach
Activates low-rank components selectively across transformers to trade compute against representational capacity.
Themes
Rank adaptation; efficient transformers; controllable capacity.

DTO-KD

ICML 2026

DTO-KD treats distillation as live negotiation between teacher gradients and task gradients. A teacher can help the student, but teacher supervision can also conflict with the downstream objective or dominate the update. The concrete object is a pair of gradient fields with possible conflict and imbalance. Dynamic balancing decides when to trust teacher information and when task evidence should dominate. The first-principles problem is useful inheritance: a student should absorb structure from the teacher only where it improves the target behavior, not obey the teacher as a fixed auxiliary loss.

Mathematical object
A pair of task and distillation gradient fields with possible conflict and dominance.
Approach
Balances gradient contributions dynamically so teacher supervision helps without overpowering task learning.
Themes
Knowledge distillation; gradient balancing; multi-objective training.

AutoEP

ICML 2026

AutoEP treats optimizer configuration as an online decision, not a fixed recipe chosen before search begins. A metaheuristic's best hyperparameters depend on the landscape it is currently encountering, including whether progress is smooth, rugged, stalled, or deceptive. The concrete object is a metaheuristic search trajectory with online landscape features and adaptive hyperparameters. Live exploratory landscape signals and multi-LLM reasoning update the search controls. The first-principles problem is feedback control: the optimizer should change its behavior from evidence gathered during search, not from assumptions made before the landscape was seen.

Mathematical object
A metaheuristic search trajectory with online landscape features and adaptive hyperparameters.
Approach
Uses live exploratory landscape signals and multi-LLM reasoning to update search parameters during optimization.
Themes
Adaptive search; optimizer control; landscape-aware hyperparameters.
BATCH 11

Representation Geometry and Latent Structure

Single-Head Attention in High Dimensions

ICML 2026

Single-Head Attention in High Dimensions treats attention as recoverable spectral geometry. Attention heads are often described as association mechanisms, but in a solvable high-dimensional setting the learned query-key spectrum determines what information can be recovered. The concrete object is the singular spectrum of learned attention matrices. The theory connects those spectral directions to interpolation, recovery thresholds, and test error. The first-principles problem is geometry of association: an attention head generalizes through the directions it learns to compare, and those directions can be studied as matrix structure rather than mystery behavior.

Mathematical object
The singular spectrum of learned query-key attention matrices in a high-dimensional model.
Approach
Derives how spectral directions govern interpolation, recovery, and test error in a solvable attention setting.
Themes
Attention theory; spectral geometry; generalization thresholds.

Gaussian SIM

ICML 2026

Gaussian SIM treats representation learning as the search for the projection that carries the response. In a single-index model, the useful signal lies along one direction and then passes through a nonlinear link. The concrete object is a projection direction and univariate link function under Gaussian inputs. Alternating gradient flow learns the direction and the link together and proves convergence in this clean setting. The first-principles problem is shared discovery: the representation and predictor must cooperate, because fitting the link is useless without the right direction and the direction is useless without the response rule.

Mathematical object
A projection direction and univariate link function in a Gaussian single-index model.
Approach
Analyzes alternating gradient flow to show convergence of direction learning and link fitting.
Themes
Single-index models; projection learning; representation dynamics.

Uncovering Latent Potential

ICML 2026

Uncovering Latent Potential treats fine-tuning as a risk to the geometry that made a representation reusable. A target metric can improve while isotropy, separability, or transfer structure quietly degrades in the embedding space. The concrete object is an embedding geometry measured by spectral properties, isotropy, and discriminative structure. Spectral layer selection and geometric regularization preserve that structure during adaptation. The first-principles problem is preserving optionality: a model should learn the new task without collapsing the latent space that lets future tasks still separate, transfer, and reuse what was learned before.

Mathematical object
An embedding geometry measured by isotropy, discriminative structure, and layerwise spectral properties.
Approach
Selects layers spectrally and regularizes geometry so fine-tuning preserves reusable latent structure.
Themes
Embedding geometry; fine-tuning; transfer preservation.

Dynamics Reveals Structure

ICML 2026

Dynamics Reveals Structure treats model editing as a question about how an update travels through relations. A local edit can fix one fact while failing to produce the composed consequences that reasoning would require. The concrete object is a representation-space update propagated through composed relational structure. First-order update dynamics can hit obstructions when relations must be chained. The first-principles problem is consequence preservation: changing a model should change the connected structure implied by the fact, not only the isolated answer that was directly edited.

Mathematical object
A representation-space update propagated through composed relational structure.
Approach
Analyzes first-order update dynamics to identify composition obstructions in editing and reasoning.
Themes
Model editing; relational reasoning; representation dynamics.

Wasserstein GPCA

ICLR 2026

Wasserstein GPCA asks how to describe variation when each data point is a distribution. Ordinary PCA assumes vectors in Euclidean space, but probability measures differ by how mass moves, not only by coordinate subtraction. The concrete object is a Wasserstein manifold of absolutely continuous measures connected by geodesics. The method lifts Gaussian-style computations through invertible maps and neural geodesics to recover principal-component structure for distributions. The first-principles idea is that a direction of variation should mean a transport path that changes one measure into another, not a line through vector coordinates.

Mathematical object
A Wasserstein distributional manifold of absolutely continuous measures connected by geodesics.
Approach
Uses invertible maps and neural geodesics to generalize PCA-style structure to probability measures.
Themes
Optimal transport; distribution geometry; neural geodesics.

NSE Index Models

ICML 2026

NSE Index Models treats learnability as more than whether useful signal exists in the data. Single- and multi-index models may contain enough statistical information in principle while remaining hard for a practical learning process to recover. The concrete object is an index model with activation-dependent statistical and computational thresholds. The analysis identifies an activation-driven exponent that governs this gap. The first-principles problem is recoverable signal: representation learning depends not only on dimension and samples, but on how the nonlinear function exposes or hides the useful direction.

Mathematical object
Single- and multi-index models with activation-dependent statistical and computational thresholds.
Approach
Derives an activation-driven exponent that predicts when representation recovery becomes computationally hard.
Themes
Index models; computational-statistical gaps; nonlinear representation learning.

Stochastic Transformers

ICML 2026

Stochastic Transformers treat initialization noise as a force that shapes representation geometry. Randomness is often dismissed as nuisance variation, but in some transformer dynamics it prevents deterministic collapse into one cluster and creates separated attractors. The concrete object is transformer representation dynamics under random initialization. The analysis shows when stochasticity changes the qualitative behavior of the learned space. The first-principles point is that noise can be structural. It may decide whether the model's internal states collapse together or separate into useful regions for later computation.

Mathematical object
Transformer representation dynamics with random initialization and possible attractor structure.
Approach
Analyzes how stochastic initialization prevents collapse and creates separated attractors in training dynamics.
Themes
Transformer theory; stochastic dynamics; representation collapse.

InfoNCE Gaussian

ICLR 2026

InfoNCE Gaussian gives contrastive embeddings a probabilistic interpretation. Positive and negative pairs explain the training rule, but they do not by themselves describe the shape of the learned space. The concrete object is a high-dimensional contrastive representation distribution treated as approximately Gaussian. Under that view, quantities such as likelihood, entropy, and mutual information become measurable rather than metaphorical. The first-principles move is to connect geometry to probability: clusters, margins, and similarity scores matter because they imply a distribution of representation mass, not only because they look separated in a plot.

Mathematical object
An approximately Gaussian high-dimensional contrastive representation distribution.
Approach
Derives likelihood, entropy, and mutual-information quantities for Gaussian-modeled InfoNCE embeddings.
Themes
Contrastive learning; probabilistic geometry; mutual information.

Compositional Generalization Requires Linear Orthogonal Representations

ICML 2026

Compositional Generalization Requires Linear Orthogonal Representations' core concept is that reliable recombination needs untangled concept coordinates. A model cannot form new combinations from known parts if the representation stores those parts as inseparable mixtures. The first-principles problem is naming the geometry required for systematic generalization: each concept must have a direction or subspace that can be changed without corrupting the others. The paper derives linear per-concept decomposition and orthogonality as necessary structure. The evidence is theoretical, connecting an abstract generalization claim to concrete geometry inside the learned representation rather than to benchmark success alone.

Mathematical object
A representation space decomposed into linear, orthogonal per-concept components.
Approach
Derives necessary orthogonal decomposition conditions for reliable recombination of learned concepts.
Themes
Compositionality; disentanglement; systematic generalization.

Neuron-Basis Circuits

ICML 2026

Neuron-Basis Circuits asks when individual neurons are more than arbitrary coordinates. Representation spaces can often be rotated, which makes any single direction hard to treat as a real mechanism. But some computations may be carried by small native neuron sets whose removal or editing changes the behavior. The concrete object is a neuron subset that causally controls grammatical agreement or multi-hop factual reasoning. The paper tests those sets by intervention. The first-principles standard is falsifiability: a circuit explanation should predict what changes when the proposed basis elements are changed.

Mathematical object
Small neuron subsets acting as causal basis elements for grammatical and factual reasoning mechanisms.
Approach
Intervenes on native neuron sets to test whether they control specific linguistic and reasoning computations.
Themes
Mechanistic interpretability; causal circuits; representation bases.

Low-Rank LM Logits

ICML 2026

Low-Rank LM Logits asks whether the model's visible output space is much smaller than it looks. A language model scores thousands of tokens, but across related prompts those scores may vary along only a limited number of directions. The concrete object is a prompt-response logit matrix whose approximate rank is far below the vocabulary dimension. The paper measures this structure and gives theory for why it appears. The first-principles point is that many token probabilities may be governed by a compressed output geometry, so behavior can be studied through fewer latent axes than the vocabulary suggests.

Mathematical object
Prompt-response logit matrices with low approximate rank relative to vocabulary dimension.
Approach
Empirically measures logit-rank structure and derives theoretical predictions for low-rank output behavior.
Themes
Language-model logits; low-rank structure; output-space geometry.

Latent Space Dynamics

ICLR 2026

Latent Space Dynamics reads prior knowledge from attractors in latent vector fields. A representation is not only a table of embeddings; it can define a dynamical system whose stable points reveal what the model treats as likely, recoverable, or natural. The concrete object is a latent vector field with attractors that encode stable prior structure. Studying those attractors exposes model knowledge before a new input is supplied. The first-principles problem is prior extraction: ask what the model's internal dynamics settle toward when left to evolve, because those endpoints reveal assumptions built into the representation.

Mathematical object
A latent vector field with attractors that encode stable prior knowledge.
Approach
Analyzes latent-space attractor structure to extract prior information without input data.
Themes
Latent dynamics; prior knowledge; representation attractors.
BATCH 12

Learned Search and Geometric Dynamics

FlowOptimizer

ICML 2026

FlowOptimizer treats optimization as motion. Instead of choosing fixed mutation rules, step sizes, or selection formulas, it learns a velocity field that moves a population of candidate solutions through the search space. The concrete state is the current population together with objective values, gradients, and summary information about where search has gone. The first-principles question is whether the rule for moving can itself be learned from problem structure. The paper turns population optimization into a dynamical system whose direction adapts to the landscape, rather than a fixed recipe applied everywhere.

Mathematical object
A population state evolving under a learned velocity field conditioned on objective and gradient information.
Approach
Trains movement rules for candidate populations so iterative optimization becomes learned dynamics.
Themes
Learned optimization; population search; velocity-field dynamics.

ABOM

ICML 2026

ABOM adapts evolutionary operators while solving the real black-box problem. Fixed mutation or search rules can be brittle because the target landscape may differ from handcrafted settings or offline meta-training tasks. The concrete object is an evolutionary population with operator parameters updated from current population evidence. The optimizer changes its mutation and exploration behavior online as it learns the live landscape. The first-principles problem is search self-calibration: the method should tune how it explores from the problem it is actually solving, not from assumptions about what black-box landscapes usually look like.

Mathematical object
An evolutionary search population with online-adapted operator parameters.
Approach
Updates evolutionary operators from current target-task population statistics instead of handcrafted meta-training tasks.
Themes
Black-box optimization; online adaptation; evolutionary search.

Controlled LLM Training on Spectral Sphere

ICML 2026

Controlled LLM Training on Spectral Sphere treats stable scaling as a geometric constraint on weights and updates. Large-model training must control function movement and activation statistics together, especially when width and depth change. The concrete object is a set of weights and optimizer updates constrained to spectral spheres. The method aligns steepest descent with muP-style activation stability by shaping update geometry. The first-principles problem is scale-compatible motion: as a model grows, the training step should move the function predictably instead of changing behavior because the parameter scale changed.

Mathematical object
Weights and optimizer updates constrained to spectral spheres for stable large-model scaling.
Approach
Uses spectral-sphere constraints to align steepest descent with muP-style activation stability.
Themes
LLM training theory; spectral constraints; stable scaling.

L2Seg

ICML 2026

L2Seg reuses local certainty inside iterative combinatorial search. Route solvers waste effort when they repeatedly reconsider segments that have already stabilized, but freezing the whole route too early can lock in mistakes. The concrete object is a route decomposed into stable and unstable segments, with stable segments aggregated as hypernodes. Predicting segment stability lets later search operate over larger reliable units while continuing to refine uncertain parts. The first-principles problem is selective commitment: a solver should remember substructure that is already trustworthy without pretending the entire solution is settled.

Mathematical object
A route solution decomposed into stable and unstable segments, with stable segments aggregated as hypernodes.
Approach
Predicts segment stability and lets iterative solvers reuse reliable substructure during combinatorial search.
Themes
Combinatorial optimization; route search; local-certainty reuse.

PCD

ICML 2026

PCD pushes a learned generator beyond the static support that trained it. In discovery tasks, a generator that only reproduces familiar candidates can be safe but useless, because the target may lie in a new high-performing region. The concrete object is a generator-induced candidate distribution steered toward novel high-value samples. The method adds search pressure while preserving useful learned structure. The first-principles problem is controlled extrapolation: a generator should become a launch point for exploration, not a boundary that prevents the search from leaving previously observed examples.

Mathematical object
A generator-induced candidate distribution steered toward novel high-performing regions.
Approach
Adds discovery pressure so generated samples move beyond training support while preserving useful structure.
Themes
Generative optimization; extrapolation; discovery search.

SecondOrderSmoothCruiser

ICML 2026

SecondOrderSmoothCruiser measures optimization difficulty through the accuracy of local higher-order models. A first-order smoothness constant can hide whether the Taylor approximation near the current point is precise enough for reliable progress. The concrete object is the local Taylor remainder that controls oracle complexity. The analysis shows how second-order and higher-order smoothness govern SmoothCruiser-style methods. The first-principles point is that algorithmic difficulty is not captured by one generic smoothness number. It depends on how much of the function's local behavior the optimizer can predict before choosing the next query.

Mathematical object
Local Taylor remainders controlling oracle complexity for higher-order smooth optimization.
Approach
Analyzes how second-order and higher-order smoothness determine SmoothCruiser-style optimization complexity.
Themes
Higher-order optimization; oracle complexity; local smoothness.

DeepWalk Trajectory

ICML 2026

DeepWalk Trajectory treats a graph embedding as something formed over time, not only as a final point cloud. Random walks expose local neighborhoods, and skip-gram negative sampling gradually turns those co-occurrences into geometry. The concrete object is a training trajectory over graph-walk embeddings under a stochastic block model. The analysis asks when that trajectory amplifies community structure enough for clusters to be recovered. The first-principles problem is emergence of structure: a graph learner should be judged by how training makes hidden communities visible, not only by the final embedding picture.

Mathematical object
A skip-gram negative-sampling trajectory over graph-walk embeddings under a stochastic block model.
Approach
Tracks optimization dynamics to derive when graph clusters become recoverable from learned embeddings.
Themes
Graph representation learning; optimization trajectories; cluster recovery.

Fisher Memory Dynamics

ICML 2026

Fisher Memory Dynamics separates useful memory from generic dynamical richness. A recurrent or state-space model can sit near a complex critical regime and still fail to preserve the input-output directions a task needs. The concrete object is a stable dynamical subspace measured by Fisher geometry and alignment with the target computation. The work asks whether the system's long-lived directions carry task-relevant information or only interesting internal motion. The first-principles point is that memory is valuable when it preserves the right distinctions over time, not when the dynamics merely look rich.

Mathematical object
Stable dynamical subspaces measured by Fisher geometry and input-output alignment.
Approach
Compares criticality with task-aligned stability to explain when recurrent memory is actually useful.
Themes
Memory dynamics; recurrent systems; Fisher geometry.

BBP Transitions

ICML 2026

BBP Transitions study the point where a hidden signal becomes visible in the spectrum of learning. In teacher-student models, planted structure can be buried inside noisy curvature, so eigenvalues look like background variation rather than information. The concrete object is the Hessian spectrum and the outliers that appear when a BBP-style transition is crossed. The paper identifies when those outliers begin to carry recoverable signal. This connects random matrix theory to representation learning by asking when curvature stops being mere training noise and starts revealing the structure the model can use.

Mathematical object
Hessian spectra with outlier transitions in teacher-student representation learning.
Approach
Uses BBP transition analysis to identify when planted signal becomes recoverable from curvature outliers.
Themes
Random matrix theory; Hessian spectra; signal recovery.

Language Symmetry Geometry

ICML 2026

Language Symmetry Geometry explains why embedding spaces can develop recognizable shapes. Circles, lines, and analogy-like directions need not be accidental artifacts of training; they can follow from translation symmetries in word co-occurrence statistics. The concrete object is embedding geometry induced by those statistical symmetries. The paper derives how regularities in language data produce structured directions in representation space. The first-principles point is that geometry should be tied back to the data-generating pattern. An embedding shape matters when it reflects a stable relation in language, not merely when it looks interesting after projection.

Mathematical object
Embedding geometry induced by translation symmetries in language co-occurrence statistics.
Approach
Derives how statistical symmetries generate circles, lines, and structured directions in embeddings.
Themes
Language embeddings; symmetry; analogy geometry.

Riemannian Metric Matching

ICML 2026

Riemannian Metric Matching treats a diffusion model as carrying an implicit geometry that must be recovered from its behavior. In latent space, distance shapes sampling, interpolation, and uncertainty, but the right metric may not be given by an explicit graph. The concrete object is a Riemannian metric represented through the carre du champ operator of a diffusion process. Denoising behavior is used to estimate that metric directly. The first-principles problem is learned distance: infer which states the generator treats as near or far instead of assuming Euclidean geometry is the truth.

Mathematical object
A Riemannian metric represented through the carre du champ operator of a diffusion process.
Approach
Uses denoising to learn metric structure directly, avoiding a pre-specified graph over latent states.
Themes
Diffusion geometry; Riemannian metrics; latent-space distances.

Embedding Translation

ICML 2026

Embedding Translation studies what is lost when meaning is moved between latent coordinate systems. Retrieval, routing, and cross-model tools often treat embeddings from different models as if a learned translation makes them interchangeable. The concrete object is a translation between embedding spaces, including out-of-distribution inputs and chains of multiple translations. The paper analyzes how geometric error grows when coordinate mismatch is ignored. The first-principles warning is that meaning is not a free vector payload. It is represented relative to a space, and converting spaces can distort the relations that made the vector useful.

Mathematical object
Translations between embedding spaces with out-of-distribution and chained geometric error.
Approach
Studies how mixed-model and chained embedding translations amplify coordinate-system mismatch.
Themes
Embedding interoperability; retrieval geometry; cross-model representation translation.
BATCH 13

Representation Expressivity and Symmetry

Detecting the Semantic Fixed Point

ICML 2026

Detecting the Semantic Fixed Point asks when a transformer has already settled on the meaning it needs. Each layer changes the hidden state, but the sequence of hidden states can be read as an iterative process moving toward a stable semantic point. The concrete object is that trajectory through depth. The method measures its geometry to decide when more layers no longer change the representation enough to matter. The first-principles stopping rule is internal convergence: inference can exit because the representation has stabilized, not because a fixed layer budget or vocabulary-specific confidence rule says to stop.

Mathematical object
A Transformer hidden-state trajectory through depth with convergence toward a semantic fixed point.
Approach
Measures trajectory geometry to detect internal stabilization and trigger vocabulary-independent early exit.
Themes
Inference efficiency; depth dynamics; representation convergence.

Which Algorithms Can GNNs Learn

ICML 2026

Which Algorithms Can GNNs Learn treats graph algorithm learning as a question about which relational distinctions survive message passing. A GNN cannot learn an algorithm if its update rule collapses graph states that the algorithm must keep separate. The concrete object is a message-passing representation and the information it preserves across rounds. The work characterizes algorithm classes standard GNNs cannot represent and designs stronger variants. The first-principles problem is expressivity before data: no amount of training examples can teach an algorithm whose required distinctions the architecture erases.

Mathematical object
Message-passing graph representations and the relational distinctions they preserve across rounds.
Approach
Characterizes algorithm classes standard GNNs cannot represent and designs variants with stronger expressivity.
Themes
Graph neural networks; algorithmic reasoning; representation expressivity.

Discrete Geometry of ReLU Networks

ICML 2026

Discrete Geometry of ReLU Networks treats expressivity as the structure of a partitioned space, not only a count of regions. ReLU networks divide input space into polyhedral cells, and the connectivity among those cells affects how the learned function can change across paths. The concrete object is a polyhedral region complex with a connectivity graph. Average-degree bounds describe that graph more precisely than raw region counts. The first-principles problem is combinatorial shape: a piecewise-linear network is powerful because of how its local linear pieces are arranged and connected, not merely because there are many of them.

Mathematical object
A polyhedral region complex and its connectivity graph induced by ReLU activations.
Approach
Bounds average degree in region-connectivity graphs to characterize piecewise-linear function geometry.
Themes
ReLU theory; discrete geometry; neural expressivity.

RECM

ICLR 2026

RECM treats equivariance as a commitment justified by the data distribution, not as a rule to impose everywhere. Symmetry helps when the world truly respects it, but forced symmetry can block asymmetric behavior that the task needs. The concrete object is a representation class that becomes fully equivariant on symmetric distributions and remains flexible elsewhere. The method gives recovery conditions for when symmetry should emerge. The first-principles problem is conditional invariance: keep transformations that preserve meaning when the data support them, and allow non-symmetric solutions when they do not.

Mathematical object
A representation class that can be fully equivariant on symmetric distributions and flexible elsewhere.
Approach
Designs recovery conditions that enforce symmetry only when the underlying data distribution supports it.
Themes
Equivariance; distributional symmetry; flexible representations.

OENN/CENN

ICML 2026

OENN/CENN's core concept is equivariant approximation beyond ordinary group actions. Many structured domains contain transformations that compose but cannot be undone, such as forgetting detail, projecting structure, or moving between object types. Standard group-equivariant networks assume invertible transformations, so they miss this kind of structure. The first-principles problem is function approximation with one-way symmetries: if the input is transformed by a compositional rule, the output should transform consistently. OENN/CENN extends equivariant universal approximation to categorical symmetries, giving a cleaner theory for neural maps whose structure is compositional without being group-like.

Mathematical object
Non-invertible compositional categorical symmetries and neural maps equivariant to them.
Approach
Proves universal approximation results for equivariant networks under categorical rather than group-only structure.
Themes
Categorical symmetry; equivariant approximation; structured representations.

PanoWorld-X

ICML 2026

PanoWorld-X controls scene generation through camera-ray geometry rather than flat image coordinates. Large-motion panoramic generation has to preserve how views move through physical space; otherwise the world can look locally plausible while drifting globally. The concrete object is a panoramic Plucker ray embedding that encodes view direction and scene geometry. The method conditions generation on these ray coordinates so motion remains spatially coherent. The first-principles problem is choosing the right coordinate system: a generated world should be organized by rays through space, not only by pixels on a rectangular image plane.

Mathematical object
Panoramic Plucker ray embeddings encoding view direction and large-motion scene geometry.
Approach
Uses ray-coordinate embeddings to condition and control panoramic scene generation under large motion.
Themes
Spatial generation; ray geometry; panoramic world models.

Context-Parameter Equivalence

ICML 2026

Context-Parameter Equivalence asks when a prompt can do the same job as a weight update. Extra examples in context may change the model's answers, but that does not automatically mean they give the same control as fine-tuning. The concrete object is the model's input-output function: which changes in that function can be caused by context alone, and which require parameter movement? The paper studies this through controllability. Its value is the boundary: prompting is powerful when context spans the needed functional change, and limited when it cannot reach that change.

Mathematical object
Input-output controllability conditions connecting context changes to parameter-update effects.
Approach
Analyzes when in-context examples induce the same functional movement as changing parameters.
Themes
In-context learning; adaptation theory; function-space control.

Symmetry ICL Dynamics

ICLR 2026

Symmetry ICL Dynamics uses symmetry as a way to expose what in-context learning is doing. If a task does not depend on the order of examples or on arbitrary label names, the learning rule should respect those swaps. The concrete object is a transformer whose internal updates are constrained by feature and label permutation symmetry. Under those constraints, the paper derives explicit layer-by-layer recursions. The first-principles gain is clarity: symmetry removes degrees of freedom that are not part of the task, leaving a smaller mechanism whose context-learning dynamics can be written down and inspected.

Mathematical object
A Transformer layerwise recursion constrained by feature and label permutation equivariance.
Approach
Uses symmetry constraints to derive explicit in-context learning dynamics across layers.
Themes
In-context learning; equivariance; transformer dynamics.

Isotropic Gaussian RL

ICML 2026

Isotropic Gaussian RL treats representation health as balanced use of the policy's coordinates. Reinforcement learning can raise reward while allowing many neurons to go dormant or compressing behavior into a narrow subspace. That may work for the current task but leaves the agent brittle for future learning. The concrete object is representation geometry measured by coordinate balance, dormancy, and collapse. Isotropic Gaussian pressure encourages the policy to use dimensions more evenly. The first-principles goal is to preserve an adaptable basis for action, not only to maximize today's return.

Mathematical object
A policy representation geometry measured by coordinate balance, dormancy, and collapse.
Approach
Adds isotropic Gaussian pressure so reinforcement learning uses dimensions more evenly.
Themes
RL representation health; neuron dormancy; isotropic geometry.

Emergent Analogical Reasoning

ICML 2026

Emergent Analogical Reasoning treats analogy as inference over relations, not as surface similarity. Two domains may look different while sharing the same roles, transformations, or constraints. The concrete object is a correspondence map between category structures and their relations. The paper formalizes analogy as category-to-category alignment and studies when data, scale, and optimization produce representations that support it. The first-principles question is what must be preserved for transfer: the model has to map relational roles across domains, not merely notice that two examples contain similar words or objects.

Mathematical object
A correspondence map between category structures and their relations.
Approach
Formalizes analogy as relational correspondence inference and studies emergence under data, scale, and optimization.
Themes
Analogical reasoning; relational alignment; emergent capabilities.

Manifold Perturbations

ICML 2026

Manifold Perturbations treats generation as constrained motion, even when the model was trained in a larger ambient space. Diffusion and flow samplers can drift into directions that are not valid degrees of freedom for the object being generated. The concrete object is a constrained data manifold embedded in ambient space with equality constraints defining valid motion. The method perturbs sampling dynamics to respect those intrinsic constraints. The first-principles problem is valid movement: a sampler should move along the space where real objects can exist, not wander through coordinates that only exist mathematically.

Mathematical object
A constrained data manifold embedded in ambient space, with equality constraints defining valid motion.
Approach
Perturbs sampling dynamics to respect intrinsic constraints while still using ambient-space trained models.
Themes
Constrained generation; manifold sampling; diffusion and flow stability.

Diffusion Spacetime

ICLR 2026

Diffusion Spacetime treats diffusion time as part of the state, not as a label outside the geometry. If the state is only the current sample, the induced metric can degenerate near terminal noise or distort the denoising path. The concrete object is a diffusion spacetime state consisting of sample coordinates and diffusion time. Building geometry over sample-time pairs keeps the trajectory visible. The first-principles problem is path faithfulness: a diffusion model should be analyzed through the changing process that generates samples, not only through static snapshots at each noise level.

Mathematical object
A diffusion spacetime state consisting of both sample coordinates and diffusion time.
Approach
Builds geometry over sample-time pairs to avoid degenerate diffusion metrics.
Themes
Diffusion geometry; generative trajectories; spacetime representation.

ERC Loss

ICLR 2026

ERC Loss asks a plain question about mixture-of-experts models: when a token is routed to an expert, did the model learn a real division of work or only a noisy traffic pattern? Sparse experts save computation only if routing creates useful specialization. The concrete object is the distribution of tokens, skills, and internal features assigned to each expert during long pretraining. ERC-style measurement turns specialization into a quantity that can be watched and shaped, so MoE training can separate useful expert roles from accidental fragmentation before the final model is evaluated.

Mathematical object
A mixture-of-experts routing distribution with measurable expert specialization structure.
Approach
Defines and uses ERC-style signals to monitor and control expert specialization during pretraining.
Themes
Mixture-of-experts; routing geometry; specialization control.
BATCH 14

Strategic Learning and Constrained Games

Asymmetric Perturbation

ICML 2026

Asymmetric Perturbation studies what happens when only one player's incentives change. In many strategic systems, a policy, subsidy, rule, or learning update affects one side more than another, yet the designer may want the same equilibrium to remain valid. The concrete object is a game equilibrium preserved under asymmetric perturbation of one player's payoff. The method constructs payoff changes whose equilibrium set aligns with the original solution. The first-principles problem is strategic stability: a solution is stronger when it survives uneven incentive changes, not only symmetric noise.

Mathematical object
A game equilibrium preserved under asymmetric perturbation of one player's payoff.
Approach
Constructs payoff perturbations whose equilibrium set aligns with the original strategic solution.
Themes
Game theory; equilibrium robustness; incentive perturbations.

RQE Actor-Critic

ICML 2026

RQE Actor-Critic asks what equilibrium a learning system should target when perfect rationality is too sharp for finite data. Exact Nash-style endpoints can be hard to estimate and unstable when each agent is learning from samples. The concrete object is a regularized bounded-rational equilibrium used as the actor-critic target. This smoother strategic object still captures response to other agents, but it gives analysis room for finite-sample guarantees. The first-principles move is to choose an equilibrium notion that is learnable from available evidence, not only elegant as an ideal endpoint.

Mathematical object
A regularized bounded-rational equilibrium used as the target of actor-critic learning.
Approach
Provides finite-sample actor-critic guarantees by optimizing toward the smoother RQE solution concept.
Themes
Multi-agent RL; bounded rationality; finite-sample strategic learning.

Nash Equilibria with Coupling Constraints

ICML 2026

Nash Equilibria with Coupling Constraints studies games where one player's action changes what other players are allowed to do. Shared resources, safety budgets, routing limits, and markets often have this form, so independent optimization is the wrong picture. The concrete object is a Nash game with playerwise concave objectives and shared coupled feasible constraints. The proof uses feasible-set topology to show an equilibrium exists. The first-principles problem is shared feasibility: before computing a strategic outcome, we need to know that mutual best responses can coexist under the common constraint.

Mathematical object
A Nash game with playerwise concave objectives and shared coupled feasible constraints.
Approach
Uses topological feasible-set arguments to establish equilibrium existence under shared constraints.
Themes
Constrained games; equilibrium existence; shared feasibility.

FTRL Lower Bounds

ICML 2026

FTRL Lower Bounds separates eventual convergence from practical equilibrium discovery. Follow-the-regularized-leader is a standard learning dynamic, and potential games look structurally friendly, but the path to equilibrium can still be very long. The concrete object is an FTRL trajectory in a two-player potential game designed to be hard. Exponential lower bounds show that no-regret structure does not guarantee fast arrival at Nash equilibrium. The first-principles lesson is time matters: a dynamic can be theoretically well behaved while still being unusable as a mechanism for finding the strategic solution in any practical horizon.

Mathematical object
FTRL trajectories in two-player potential games with hard equilibrium-reaching instances.
Approach
Constructs lower-bound games showing exponential time can be required despite potential-game structure.
Themes
Online learning; no-regret dynamics; equilibrium complexity.

Fair OT

ICML 2026

Fair OT treats fairness as a constraint on how distributional mass moves. When examples, decisions, or representations are transported across domains, group-level constraints can be preserved or violated by the geometry of that movement. The concrete object is an optimal-transport plan with fairness penalties and learned costs. Fair Sinkhorn methods, penalized guarantees, and bilevel cost learning make the constraint part of transport itself. The first-principles problem is fairness under shift: a fairness rule should not only fit the observed sample; it should control how mass is reassigned when the model meets new data.

Mathematical object
An optimal-transport plan with fairness penalties and learned costs over source and target distributions.
Approach
Uses fair Sinkhorn and bilevel cost learning to transport mass while controlling fairness constraints.
Themes
Fairness; optimal transport; distributional constraints.

Feasible Payoffs

ICML 2026

Feasible Payoffs treats inverse game analysis as set-valued uncertainty. Observed equilibrium play can be consistent with many payoff structures, so returning one fitted reward can claim more than the data identify. The concrete object is a Hausdorff-approximated set of payoff functions consistent with observed strategic behavior. Estimating the full feasible set keeps incentive uncertainty visible. The first-principles problem is identification discipline: if behavior proves only that payoffs lie in a region, the answer should be that region, not a single utility story chosen because it is easier to report.

Mathematical object
A Hausdorff-approximated set of payoff functions consistent with observed equilibrium behavior.
Approach
Recovers feasible payoff sets rather than a single inverse-game explanation.

Inverse games; payoff uncertainty; equilibrium identification.

First-Price Auctions

ICML 2026

First-Price Auctions studies convergence while keeping approximation choices explicit. Bidding dynamics are shaped by the auction mechanism, discretized bid spaces, policy approximation, and incentive response, so a learning result is incomplete if those numerical choices disappear. The concrete object is a first-price auction learning dynamic with discretization and approximation error. Polynomial convergence rates are proved while tracking those tradeoffs. The first-principles problem is strategic numerical meaning: a learned bidding policy counts as converged only if its equilibrium claim survives the way bids and policies were represented computationally.

Mathematical object
A first-price auction learning dynamic with discretized bidding and approximation error.
Approach
Proves polynomial convergence rates while tracking discretization and approximation tradeoffs.
Themes
Auction learning; mechanism design; convergence rates.

Ranking Feedback Online Learning

ICML 2026

Ranking Feedback Online Learning starts with a missing number. Many systems learn from ordered choices: this answer was preferred to that one, or this item ranked above another. A ranking says direction, not size. The concrete object is online regret when the learner receives ordinal comparisons instead of calibrated rewards. The paper asks which guarantees survive when the feedback channel loses magnitude information. Its first-principles contribution is a boundary between possible and impossible learning: some ranking signals still guide improvement, while others simply do not contain enough information to support the same claims.

Mathematical object
An online learner receiving ordinal ranking feedback instead of numeric utility observations.
Approach
Derives regret upper and lower bounds that show exactly what ranking feedback can support.
Themes
Online learning; ranking feedback; preference information limits.

Fair Causal Bandits

ICML 2026

Fair Causal Bandits treats exploration as constrained by fairness rules that may be only partly known. A bandit learner must try actions to discover reward, but those actions can affect real subjects and violate counterfactual fairness while learning. The concrete object is a bandit policy with unknown roundwise counterfactual fairness constraints. The theory balances regret against fairness-violation bounds under causal structure. The first-principles problem is responsible experimentation: learn which actions work while treating fairness as part of the learning process, not as an audit performed after harm has occurred.

Mathematical object
A bandit policy with unknown counterfactual fairness constraints across rounds.
Approach
Balances reward learning with regret and fairness-violation guarantees under causal constraints.
Themes
Causal bandits; fairness; constrained exploration.

Loss-Aware OT-DRO

ICML 2026

Loss-Aware OT-DRO shapes robustness around the loss the decision-maker actually pays. A generic uncertainty ball can spend budget on distribution shifts that do not change the decision, while missing small movements that create large downstream loss. The concrete object is an optimal-transport ambiguity set learned with respect to that decision loss. Bilevel hypergradients tune the set toward sensitive directions in the data distribution. The first-principles point is targeted protection: robustness should defend the decision boundary where errors are costly, not treat every possible shift as equally important simply because it is mathematically nearby.

Mathematical object
An optimal-transport ambiguity set learned with respect to a downstream decision loss.
Approach
Uses bilevel hypergradients to shape DRO uncertainty around loss-sensitive distribution shifts.
Themes
Distributionally robust optimization; optimal transport; decision-focused uncertainty.

What Preferences Can and Cannot Predict

ICML 2026

What Preferences Can and Cannot Predict separates stable rankings from stable learning dynamics. Preference observations can reveal local structure, but they do not automatically say how multi-agent policies will behave once those policies start adapting. The concrete object is a comparison between preference observations and dynamic stability properties of learning systems. The work shows when preferential stability transfers to subgames and when it fails in general dynamics. The first-principles problem is limits of preference evidence: rankings can support some stability claims, but they cannot certify every future interaction among adapting agents.

ICLR 2026

GWF's core concept is understanding distributional objectives as flows. A generative method does not merely minimize a number; its chosen discrepancy defines how probability mass is pushed through space. The first-principles problem is to identify the motion implied by an objective, because different distances create different training dynamics and failure modes. GWF extends Wasserstein-flow derivations from f-divergences to integral probability metrics and squared MMD. The evidence is theoretical: objectives that looked like separate tools can be compared by the flows they induce, making the geometry of distribution change visible instead of implicit.

Mathematical object
Wasserstein flows induced by divergences, integral probability metrics, and squared MMD.
Approach
Derives flow structure for a wider class of distributional objectives beyond f-divergences.
Themes
Wasserstein geometry; generative objectives; distributional flows.

Path-dependent DAI

ICML 2026

Path-dependent DAI treats discrete construction as inference over the full history of choices. In combinatorial generation, a partial object is not just a prefix; the route used to build it changes what future moves mean and which latent dynamics are plausible. The concrete object is a path-dependent construction MDP over partial discrete objects. Lifting the sampler with latent dynamics lets future choices depend on earlier evidence, not only the current visible state. The first-principles problem is historical dependence: two identical-looking partial objects may require different next actions because they came from different construction paths.

Mathematical object
A path-dependent construction MDP with latent dynamics over partial discrete objects.
Approach
Conditions samplers on full construction histories so future choices respect earlier latent evidence.
Themes
Discrete sampling; amortized inference; path-dependent generation.

Risk Hypergraphs

ICML 2026

Risk Hypergraphs treats medical risk as interaction structure rather than a flat list of diagnoses. Electronic health records often contain disease combinations and shared factors whose joint pattern matters more than any single condition. The concrete object is a latent hypergraph of disease subsets and risk-factor interactions. Hyperedges let probabilistic inference represent pathways that independent-label models can miss. The first-principles problem is combinatorial risk: prediction should account for groups of conditions that become meaningful together, because a patient's risk state is often carried by the relation among variables, not one variable alone.

Mathematical object
A latent hypergraph of disease subsets and shared risk-factor interactions in EHR data.
Approach
Models risk through hyperedge interactions rather than independent diagnosis probabilities.
Themes
Healthcare ML; probabilistic risk; hypergraph representations.

CRC

ICLR 2026

CRC's core concept is prediction sets designed for the downstream decision, not coverage alone. A calibrated set can contain the truth at the promised rate while still being operationally poor if it protects against errors that do not matter for the action. The first-principles problem is decision-aware uncertainty: construct sets that keep the next choice robust, not merely statistically covered. CRC optimizes prediction-set construction under decision robustness constraints. The evidence is whether the set improves the action that follows, shifting uncertainty evaluation from abstract inclusion to the practical consequence of being wrong.

Mathematical object
Prediction sets constrained by downstream decision robustness rather than coverage alone.
Approach
Optimizes conformal-style sets against robustness criteria tied to the follow-on decision.
Themes
Uncertainty sets; robust decisions; conformal-style prediction.

CreDRO

ICML 2026

CreDRO's core concept is epistemic uncertainty as structured disagreement across plausible data-generating worlds. Random seed variation can make uncertainty look like training noise, even when the real question is whether several distributions could explain the data. The first-principles problem is prediction under model ambiguity: return a set that reflects what remains unknowable from available evidence. CreDRO builds credal prediction sets from distributionally robust model disagreement, so uncertainty comes from a family of plausible distributions rather than repeated runs of one learner. The evidence is whether these sets expose epistemic ambiguity more faithfully under distributional uncertainty.

Mathematical object
Credal prediction sets induced by distributionally robust model disagreement.
Approach
Constructs prediction sets from robust disagreement across plausible distributions instead of seed variance.
Themes
Credal prediction; epistemic uncertainty; robust disagreement.

p-less

ICLR 2026

p-less treats decoding diversity as a controlled distributional change, not as turning one randomness knob upward. High-temperature sampling can explore more outputs, but it can also spread probability mass in ways that damage math, reasoning, or creative coherence. The concrete object is a decoding distribution whose concentration is relaxed while useful structure is preserved. The method changes sampling behavior so exploration increases without collapsing quality. The first-principles question is where probability mass can be freed safely: enough to escape bland outputs, not so much that the model stops respecting the constraints of the task.

Mathematical object
A decoding distribution whose probability concentration is relaxed while preserving useful structure.
Approach
Changes high-temperature sampling behavior to expand diversity without collapsing reasoning quality.
Themes
Decoding; sampling diversity; reasoning generation.

LDM

ICML 2026

LDM studies when self-supervised learning recovers a real hidden structure rather than an arbitrary code. Many embeddings can predict well, but only some correspond to stable latent variables that remain meaningful across views or future observations. The concrete object is a predictive latent distribution whose matching can identify the underlying representation. The paper proves conditions under which this recovery is possible. The first-principles issue is identifiability: a learned representation should not merely be useful for a loss, but tied to the latent structure that generated the data.

Mathematical object
Predictive latent distributions whose matching identifies stable hidden representations.
Approach
Proves identifiability conditions for recovering latent structure from predictive distribution matching.
Themes
Latent representation learning; identifiability; self-supervised inference.

Ambiguity-Averse MDPs

ICML 2026

Ambiguity-Averse MDPs' core concept is robust sequential decision-making that still decomposes over time. A planner may want to avoid actions whose outcomes are uncertain because the transition model is poorly known, but many risk preferences destroy the Bellman recursion that makes planning practical. The first-principles problem is compatibility between uncertainty preference and time decomposition. This work characterizes law-invariant risk measures that preserve dynamic programming in MDPs. The evidence is the boundary it draws: some forms of ambiguity aversion remain computationally usable, while others express caution in a way that breaks tractable planning.

Mathematical object
An MDP objective with law-invariant ambiguity risk measures and Bellman decomposability.
Approach
Characterizes which risk measures preserve dynamic programming under epistemic uncertainty.
Themes
Robust RL; ambiguity aversion; dynamic programming.
BATCH 19

Scaling Laws and Capacity Limits

Length Generalization Bounds

ICLR 2026

Length Generalization Bounds treats extrapolation as a precise numerical claim. A transformer that works on short contexts may fail at longer lengths, and the answer depends on the error norm and on how attention is implemented. The concrete object is a set of transformer length-extrapolation bounds under different error metrics and attention mechanisms. The analysis separates infinity-norm error from average error and softmax attention from finite-precision attention. The first-principles problem is stated reliability: length generalization only means something when the error being controlled and the computation producing it are explicit.

Mathematical object
Transformer length extrapolation bounds under different error norms and attention implementations.
Approach
Derives bounds that separate error metric choice from softmax and finite-precision attention behavior.
Themes
Length generalization; transformer theory; finite-precision attention.

MTS Difficulty

ICML 2026

MTS Difficulty treats data difficulty as something that changes during training. A sample or task is not permanently easy or hard; its value depends on the current model, the batch around it, and how training weights have shifted. The concrete object is a set of time-varying task and sample weights in a multi-task training trajectory. The method analyzes weight dynamics and uses batch, distribution, and training features for task selection. The first-principles problem is timing of evidence: choose data according to what the model can learn from now, not a fixed difficulty label.

Mathematical object
Time-varying task and sample weights in a multi-task training trajectory.
Approach
Uses data-weight dynamics and batch/distribution features to improve multi-task selection.
Themes
Data selection; multi-task learning; training dynamics.

Coverage Principle

ICLR 2026

Coverage Principle treats post-training as amplification of behavior that must already be reachable in the base model. Best-of-N and reward optimization can look like they create capability, but they select from probability mass pretraining already assigned to candidate responses. The concrete object is pretrained probability mass on high-quality responses reachable by selection or post-training. The principle formalizes how much good response mass must exist before amplification can work. The first-principles problem is support before selection: a reward procedure can favor good answers only if the base distribution covers them enough to find.

Mathematical object
Pretrained probability mass assigned to high-quality responses reachable by selection or post-training.
Approach
Formalizes coverage needed for Best-of-N and post-training to amplify good outputs.
Themes
Pretraining distributions; post-training; capability amplification.

Intrinsic Entropy

ICLR 2026

Intrinsic Entropy treats context length as a data-supported capacity, not as a number to increase without limit. Longer context helps only when the training distribution contains enough usable long-range information for the model to learn. The concrete object is a relationship among dataset entropy, sample size, and optimal supported context length. The analysis derives limits on context scaling from the source itself. The first-principles problem is justified memory: a model should be given context it can statistically learn to use, not empty span that exceeds the evidence available in training data.

Mathematical object
A relationship among dataset entropy, sample size, and optimal supported context length.
Approach
Derives data-dependent limits on context-length scaling from intrinsic entropy considerations.
Themes
Context scaling; data entropy; sample complexity.

Multi-Epoch Scaling

ICLR 2026

Multi-Epoch Scaling separates repeated exposure from fresh evidence. When new data is scarce, training longer on the same examples can help, but it does not expand the data distribution in the way new samples do. The concrete object is a scaling comparison between K-epoch reuse and one-pass fresh-data training. The analysis measures when reuse still improves the model and when it saturates relative to novel data. The first-principles problem is compute allocation: decide whether the next unit of training should deepen optimization on known examples or broaden what the model has seen.

Mathematical object
Scaling curves comparing K-epoch data reuse with one-pass fresh-data training.
Approach
Measures when repeated exposure behaves like useful evidence and when it saturates relative to fresh data.
Themes
Data reuse; compute allocation; scaling laws.

Shallow NN Scaling Laws

ICLR 2026

Shallow NN Scaling Laws makes scaling exponents analyzable in simple networks. Large-model scaling curves are useful, but their causes are hard to isolate because data, architecture, optimization, and regularization all move together. The concrete object is an excess-risk exponent in quadratic and diagonal shallow networks. The theory shows how sample complexity and weight decay determine those exponents in a tractable setting. The first-principles value is explanation: before scaling laws become forecasting tools for huge models, simple cases should show which mathematical forces make loss shrink at a particular rate.

Mathematical object
Excess-risk scaling exponents in quadratic and diagonal shallow neural networks.
Approach
Derives how sample complexity and weight decay determine risk exponents in tractable models.
Themes
Scaling theory; simple networks; regularization.

Scaling Laws Origin

ICLR 2026

Scaling Laws Origin separates the observation of power-law learning curves from one favored explanation of them. It is tempting to say scaling laws come from power-law correlations in data, but similar curves can arise through other mechanisms. The concrete object is a set of scaling curves produced by random-graph walks and simplified language-generation processes. The work constructs cases where power-law scaling appears without power-law data correlations. The first-principles problem is causal explanation of scaling: identify what produces the curve instead of assuming the visible curve proves one data-statistical story.

Mathematical object
Scaling curves produced by random-graph walks and simplified language-generation processes.
Approach
Constructs settings where power-law scaling appears without power-law data correlations.
Themes
Scaling-law theory; data statistics; language generators.

Prescriptive Scaling

ICLR 2026

Prescriptive Scaling uses scaling analysis to guide allocation decisions. A curve fit is descriptive if it only says what happened; it becomes prescriptive when it tells where more scale is likely to change the frontier. The concrete object is a set of task capability frontiers tracked over time under increasing model scale. The paper compares which frontiers stay stable and which continue to move, with math reasoning remaining more active. The first-principles question is where added compute buys new capability rather than only making an already-stable task slightly cleaner.

Mathematical object
Task capability frontiers tracked over time under increasing scale.
Approach
Compares frontier movement across task families to guide where scale is still likely to matter.
Themes
Capability forecasting; scaling strategy; task frontiers.

Pre-training under Infinite Compute

ICLR 2026

Pre-training under Infinite Compute treats a method's limit as different from its score under one compute budget.
